chapter: Life on the road in the South
title: Finding lodging under segregation and Effie Cox's place in Lake Charles
summary: Even famous musicians had trouble finding rooms before and after 1954; she praises Effie Cox's place where Ellington's band stayed.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I see. All right. So were there any other experiences of any kind out of the ordinary with travelling with the bands during that period that stand out in your memory?

Well, the one bad experience was of course living places, living quarters. You know, you had a difficult time trying to find a nice place to stay, and I don't care who you were, how big you were, how famous or popular you were, you just didn't stay in, you know, certain places. So --
This was true even after you were famous?
Well, it was of course, up until, even after 19 -- was it '54, when the segregation thing, you know, was passed, the segregation law. Well, even up until that time.

Well, of course they still had separate facilities after that, even on busses, because I remember in Texas in '56 or '57, separate waiting rooms, I was there, and a separate section of the bus. And my husband and child and I sat in the back of the bus because we were travelling with a baby and the back seat was empty and we weren't depriving anyone of a seat and it was just more comfortable for us to let the baby lie down.
But legally it wasn't right.
And we got more looks and told we
couldn't sit there.
Yeah.
Because here we were in the back of the bus when we were supposed to be in the front of the bus.
Right, right.
And everybody looked scared.
Uh-huh. Well, they were.
You know?

They were. It was a terrible thing, you know. It really -- you know, when you stop to think about it now and I guess it's a marvelous thing to have lived through this, because so many people today, the youngsters today, they only read about this. They really can't imagine what it was like. They really can't. But to be able to say that you have lived through this and had this actual experience, well it really was something. It was something.
So when you went to a town, if you knew someone or if someone had made arrangements and they knew you were coming, there'd be a place in private homes, but --
Yeah, in private homes. This is right.
Were there times when there weren't any places arranged for? What did you do?
Well, you just wouldn't sleep or maybe you'd just have to stay in the car until somebody arranged a place, you know. But there was no such thing as

going to a hotel. And a lot of the houses, if there were rooming houses, you know, maybe some rooming houses or something, if you were lucky you could get in those places. And sometimes they weren't really, you know, really kosher.
Were there ever colored hotels in the south?

There were a few. Not -- they weren't really hotels. You know, they called them hotels, but they weren't really, but they were quarters. I'd rather call them quarters, that's really what they were. Now, for instance in my little home town we had a place in Lake Charles, and this place was called Cox, Effie Cox. Mrs. Cox's place was one of the nicest places. I think Duke and the guys stayed there. Did you ever go through Louisiana with them?
No, I never went south with them.
You never went south with them.
No.

Well, they played in Lake Charles, and I think Ellington and some of the larger bands that came through there stayed at this particular place in Lake Charles. She had a terrific place, and it was an old place, but she kept it up beautifully, it was nicely furnished, she had a restaurant, she had good food and it was just a class, a really nice, class spot.
